title: Ezekiel 26:15–21
context: The Lord GOD speaks to Tyre of the shock of her fall: the islands will shake at the sound of it, when the wounded groan and the slaughter is made within her. The princes of the sea will come down from their thrones, lay aside their robes and their embroidered garments, clothe themselves with trembling, sit on the ground, and be astonished. They will take up a lamentation: “How you are destroyed, who were inhabited by seafaring men, the renowned city, who was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who caused their terror to be on all who lived there!” The islands will tremble in the day of her fall and be dismayed at her departure. When the LORD makes her a desolate city, when he brings up the deep and the great waters cover her, he will bring her down with those who descend into the pit, to the people of old time, to dwell in the lower parts of the earth, in the places desolate of old, so that she is not inhabited; and he will set glory in the land of the living, and will make her a terror, and she will no more have any being. Though she is sought for, she will never be found again. The pit and the lower parts of the earth name the place of the dead, among the people of old time. Glory is set in the land of the living, over against that descent; the verse does not name who receives that glory. The slaughter and the groaning of the wounded are named and are not described further.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says to Tyre: ‘Won’t the islands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when the slaughter is made within you?
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says to Tyre, “Won’t the islands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when the slaughter is made within you?” The fall has a sound, and the islands shake at it. The wounded groan, and a slaughter is made within her. Those clauses name the cost of the fall and do not go on into a scene. The question expects the islands to shake.

Arminian readers hear a fall loud enough to trouble the islands, a groaning and a slaughter within the city, a word that still addresses Tyre as the one whose fall will be heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the shaking of the islands at the sound of the fall, the groaning of the wounded, and the slaughter made within her as the Lord GOD’s own picture of the shock of that day.

Shared ground: the islands shake, and there is groaning and slaughter within. The description is limited to those words.

verses.text: Then all the princes of the sea will come down from their thrones, and lay aside their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling. They will sit on the ground, and will tremble every moment, and be astonished at you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then all the princes of the sea will come down from their thrones, and lay aside their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling. They will sit on the ground, and will tremble every moment, and be astonished at you.” The sea’s princes leave their thrones, put off their fine garments, put on trembling, and sit on the ground, astonished. The pomp of the coast is undone in a moment of fear, a dirge already in posture before the words of the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a court of the sea brought down to the ground, trembling every moment, a fear that answers Tyre’s old terror, and a sign to the watching coasts that her strength is gone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the descent from the thrones, the laid-aside robes, the clothing with trembling, the sitting on the ground, and the astonishment as the Lord GOD’s appointed response of the princes of the sea.

Shared ground: the princes of the sea sit on the ground and tremble. Their glory is taken off, and they are astonished at Tyre.

verses.text: They will take up a lamentation over you, and tell you, “How you are destroyed, who were inhabited by seafaring men, the renowned city, who was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who caused their terror to be on all who lived there!”
verses.arminianNotes:
They will take up a lamentation over her, and say, “How you are destroyed, who were inhabited by seafaring men, the renowned city, who was strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who caused their terror to be on all who lived there!” The lament is in their mouths: a destroyed city, once inhabited by seafaring men, renowned, strong in the sea, a terror to all who lived there. The dirge remembers her strength in order to name her destruction, and it is the princes’ lament, reported by the LORD.

Arminian readers hear a funeral song from the coasts, a memory of seafaring strength and caused terror, now turned to “How you are destroyed,” a word Tyre is made to hear from her peers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same lamentation, the renowned city strong in the sea, the inhabitants who caused their terror, and the cry of how she is destroyed, as the song the LORD says the princes will take up.

Shared ground: the lament names what she was, and that she is destroyed. The terror she caused is part of the memory.

verses.text: Now the islands will tremble in the day of your fall. Yes, the islands that are in the sea will be dismayed at your departure.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the islands will tremble in the day of your fall. Yes, the islands that are in the sea will be dismayed at your departure.” The shaking of verse 15 becomes trembling and dismay in the day of the fall, at her departure. The sea’s islands, her natural company, are the ones dismayed. The departure is the city’s going down, already in view as a leaving of the world of the living.

Arminian readers hear a whole horizon of islands in dismay, a day of fall that does not stay private to Tyre, a word that still treats the coasts as witnesses who will feel it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the trembling of the islands in the day of the fall, and the dismay of the islands in the sea at her departure, as the Lord GOD’s own widening of the shock.

Shared ground: the islands tremble and are dismayed. The day of the fall is a day of departure.

verses.text: “For the Lord GOD says: ‘When I make you a desolate city, like the cities that are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep on you, and the great waters cover you,
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “When I make you a desolate city, like the cities that are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep on you, and the great waters cover you,” The LORD himself makes her desolate, like uninhabited cities, and brings up the deep so that the great waters cover her. The sea, her element, becomes the covering of her ruin. The sentence runs on into the descent of the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a covering by the deep, a desolation like empty cities, a judgment in the very waters that had been her strength, still spoken to Tyre as “you.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the making of a desolate city, the bringing up of the deep, and the great waters that cover her as the Lord GOD’s own act, the condition of the descent that follows.

Shared ground: the deep is brought up, and the great waters cover her. The image is the sea over a desolate city.

verses.text: then I will bring you down with those who descend into the pit, to the people of old time, and will make you dwell in the lower parts of the earth, in the places that are desolate of old, with those who go down to the pit, that you be not inhabited; and I will set glory in the land of the living.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then the LORD will bring her down with those who descend into the pit, to the people of old time, and will make her dwell in the lower parts of the earth, in the places that are desolate of old, with those who go down to the pit, so that she is not inhabited; and he will set glory in the land of the living. The pit and the lower parts of the earth name the place of the dead, among the people of old time. Glory is set in the land of the living, over against that going down; the verse does not name who receives that glory.

Arminian readers hear a descent among the long dead, a city no longer inhabited, and a glory set in the land of the living, a contrast the LORD himself draws between the pit and the living land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the bringing down to the pit, the dwelling in the lower parts of the earth with the people of old time, the end of inhabiting, and the setting of glory in the land of the living as the Lord GOD’s own act and appointment.

Shared ground: Tyre goes down to the pit, and glory is set in the land of the living. The two destinations stand in one sentence.

verses.text: I will make you a terror, and you will no more have any being. Though you are sought for, yet you will never be found again,’ says the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will make you a terror, and you will no more have any being. Though you are sought for, yet you will never be found again,” says the Lord GOD. Tyre is made a terror, and will no more have any being. Even if she is sought, she will never be found again. The close is the LORD’s, and it is final in the terms of the oracle. How later searchers have thought about the site is not a matter this verse takes up.

Arminian readers hear a city that becomes a terror and then is not found, a “never be found again” bound to the Lord GOD’s saying, a last word over the “Aha!” that began the chapter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the making of a terror, the end of her being, and the never being found again, though sought for, as the Lord GOD’s own last word in the chapter.

Shared ground: she will never be found again, and the Lord GOD has said it. The unit ends on that spoken finality.
